title: Artificial general intelligence
description: Type of hypothetical AI with wide-ranging abilities
wiki_lead:
Artificial general intelligence (AGI) is a hypothetical type of artificial intelligence that matches or surpasses human capabilities across most or all cognitive tasks. Unlike artificial narrow intelligence (ANI), whose competence is confined to well‑defined tasks, an AGI system can generalise knowledge, transfer skills between domains, and solve novel problems without task‑specific reprogramming.
Creating AGI is a stated goal of technology companies such as OpenAI, Google, SpaceXAI, and Meta. A 2020 survey identified 72 active AGI research and development projects across 37 countries.
AGI is a common topic in science fiction and futures studies.
Contention exists over whether AGI represents an existential risk. Some AI experts and industry figures have stated that mitigating the risk of human extinction posed by AGI should be a global priority. Others find the development of AGI to be in too remote a stage to present such a risk.

Terminology
AGI is also known as general AI, strong AI, full AI, human-level AI, human-level intelligent AI, or general intelligent action.
The term "artificial general intelligence" was used in 1997 by Mark Gubrud in a discussion of the implications of fully automated military production and operations. A mathematical formalism of AGI named AIXI was proposed in 2000 by Marcus Hutter, who defines intelligence as "an agent's ability to achieve goals or succeed in a wide range of environments". This type of AGI has also been called "universal artificial intelligence". The term AGI was re-introduced and popularized by Shane Legg and Ben Goertzel around 2002.
Some academic sources reserve the term "strong AI" for computer programs that will experience sentience or consciousness. In contrast, weak AI (or narrow AI) can solve a specific problem but lacks general cognitive abilities. Some academic sources use "weak AI" to refer more broadly to any programs that neither experience consciousness nor have a mind in the same sense as humans.
Related concepts include artificial superintelligence and transformative AI. An artificial superintelligence (ASI) is a hypothetical type of AGI that is much more generally intelligent than humans, while the notion of transformative AI relates to AI having a large impact on society, for example, similar to the agricultural or industrial revolution.
A framework for classifying AGI was proposed in 2023 by Google DeepMind researchers. They define five performance levels of AGI: emerging, competent, expert, virtuoso, and superhuman. For example, a competent AGI is defined as an AI that outperforms 50% of skilled adults in a wide range of non-physical tasks, and a superhuman AGI (i.e., an artificial superintelligence) is similarly defined but with a threshold of 100%. They consider large language models like ChatGPT or LLaMA 2 to be instances of emerging AGI (comparable to unskilled humans). grok_lead: There is no single universally accepted definition of artificial general intelligence (AGI) as of October 2026. It is commonly described as a hypothetical type of artificial intelligence capable of understanding, learning, reasoning, and applying knowledge across essentially any intellectual task a human being can perform, at a level matching or exceeding typical human performance, with the ability to transfer skills to novel domains without task-specific retraining. Competing operationalizations include capability matching or exceeding humans across virtually all cognitive tasks, OpenAIâs characterization (in its charter) of highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work, Google DeepMindâs 2023 Levels of AGI framework, which distinguishes performance depth (Emerging, Competent, Expert, Exceptional, Superhuman) from generality breadth, and a 2025 psychometric framework that defines AGI as matching the cognitive versatility and proficiency of a well-educated adult across ten CattellâHornâCarroll domains. The definition remains unsettled in part because these operationalizations measure different quantitiesâeconomic output, cognitive breadth, or percentile performanceâand because informal criteria have often receded as specialized systems mastered tasks once thought to require human intellect. Whether an existing system counts as AGI therefore depends on which definition is applied. AGI exhibits flexibility and generality across diverse domains rather than specialization in narrow functions. Unlike current artificial narrow intelligence (ANI)âthe only form of AI deployed at scale as of 2026âwhich is specialized for bounded tasks such as language modeling, image recognition, or game-playing, AGI would exhibit flexible, general-purpose intelligence, common-sense reasoning, continual learning, and robust adaptation. The pursuit of AGI dates to the origins of AI research in the mid-20th century, with early visions of machines matching human cognition, though progress has been intermittent amid periods of optimism and setback known as AI summers and winters. As of October 2026, no system has achieved broad scientific consensus as AGI. Current frontier models show strong but uneven (âjaggedâ) performance across many domains while remaining limited in reliable generalization, long-horizon agency, and efficient acquisition of entirely new skills. Some researchers, including UC San Diego faculty in a 2026 Nature comment, argue that advanced large language models already meet reasonable criteria for general intelligence and therefore qualify as AGI. Some industry statements have gone further: OpenAI president Greg Brockman described the September 2026 launch of GPT-6 Astra as the start of the âAGI era,â and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an August 2026 interview that the company expected an internal system he would call AGI by the end of 2026. The stronger expert consensus is that AGI has not been achieved. Stanford HAI faculty predicted there would be no AGI in 2026, and contemporary large language models and multimodal AI, while surpassing humans on certain isolated benchmarks, still lack robust generalization, causal understanding, and reliable performance in novel scenarios requiring integrated intelligence. A March 2025 AAAI Presidential Panel survey of 475 AI researchers found that 76% considered it âunlikelyâ or âvery unlikelyâ that scaling current approaches would yield AGI. Google DeepMindâs Levels of AGI framework distinguishes performance depth from generality breadth; current frontier systems are generally placed at the Emerging level. Timeline forecasts remain widely dispersed. The AI Impacts Expert Survey on Progress in AI, conducted in December 2024 among 1,580 researchers, implied a 50% chance of high-level machine intelligence by 2042; as of October 2026, Metaculus community forecasts put a 50% chance of a general AI system around November 2030, while a May 2026 expert panel (LEAP Wave 8) using a stricter occupational and cost-based definition reported a median of 2050. Some industry leaders anticipate earlier breakthroughs driven by scaling compute and data, while others highlight architectural limitations and diminishing returns. AGI development is widely discussed in terms of both opportunities and risks, which are often conflated. Laboratories and some economists argue that systems matching or exceeding human performance across cognitive tasks could raise economic productivity, accelerate scientific and medical discovery, and extend individual capabilities, if the systems remain controllable and broadly accessible. Near-term alignment and control problemsâspecification gaming, unreliable generalization, and reward hackingâare already documented in existing systems and are distinct from hypothesized existential risks from future superintelligent agents. Safety researchers including Yoshua Bengio and Stuart Russell argue that no known method would keep such future systems reliably aligned, so control should be solved before capabilities are scaled. Scaling-oriented laboratories treat benefit delivery and iterative safety work as jointly achievable, while skeptics such as Yann LeCun reject extinction scenarios as ungrounded in the properties of current or foreseeable architectures. A 2025 survey found AI experts clustered into âcontrollable toolâ and âuncontrollable agentâ viewpoints; the 2024 Expert Survey on Progress in AI reported an 18% average probability of extinction or similarly severe disempowerment from future AI, with most respondents assigning at least a 10% chance. Peer-reviewed analyses therefore emphasize empirical work on value alignment, control, and governance rather than treating any single narrative as settled.
